title: Kshamavani, the Jain day
hook: at the end of Paryushana, Jains ask forgiveness of all beings: micchami dukkadam

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. Your line was atonement. This week ran from family feuds to your younger self, reconciling, a new telling, bedtime and the Day of Atonement. Today it closes with two words sent in every direction.

The same two words arrive from all over in one morning: a coworker's message, a cousin's post, a card from a neighbor. Micchami dukkadam. No context, no list of what went wrong, just the phrase, sent to people near and far. For Jains, it marks the day at the end of Paryushana, a season of fasting, study and self-examination. Jains call the closing day by more than one name; one of them is Kshamavani, the day of forgiveness. And the forgiveness asked for on that day doesn't stop at friends and family. It reaches every living thing.
screen: `TWO WORDS, MANY DIRECTIONS.` → `THE END OF PARYUSHANA.` → `EVERY LIVING THING.`

segments.voice: First, the phrase. Micchami dukkadam comes from Prakrit, the old language of the Jain scriptures. Jains explain it as asking that whatever wrong I did be in vain, undone, without fruit. It's a request, not a speech; nobody has to name what happened. Second, the verse behind it. Jains recite a short verse in their rite of repentance, called pratikramana. In paraphrase: I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all, and enmity with none. It goes both ways in one breath: I forgive, and forgive me. Third, how wide it reaches. In Jain teaching, all living beings means exactly that: not only people, but animals, insects, the smallest creatures, the ones harmed without anyone noticing. That fits ahimsa, the Jain teaching of doing no harm. So the asking reaches a whole world someone has moved through all year, often carelessly. Fourth, why strangers too. The message goes out to people you may not have wronged at all, or don't remember wronging. That's the point. It doesn't wait for a complaint. It assumes that in a year of living, a person steps on more toes than they know, and it clears the ground anyway: two words, sent wide, asking to start the next season clean.
screen: `LET MY WRONG BE IN VAIN.` · `I FORGIVE, AND FORGIVE ME.` · `ALL LIVING BEINGS.` · `IT DOESN'T WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT.` · then, large: `MICCHAMI DUKKADAM.`

segments.voice: Start close, and hold in mind for a few breaths one person you know you've hurt this year. Then widen to people you may have hurt without knowing, a short reply, a missed call, someone you talked over, and wider still, to the creatures whose homes your life touches, until the circle is bigger than you can see. If it fits for you, silently offer the Jain phrase, micchami dukkadam, to the whole circle, or, if you pray, do this in your prayer.
Kshamavani. The Jain day of forgiveness at the close of Paryushana, when people ask pardon of all living beings. Today's word.
Your line: micchami dukkadam. No list needed, and no one left out. Day nine hundred ninety-four, done.

notes: No public-domain English translation of the khamemi verse is quoted; the paraphrase ('I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me; friendship with all, enmity with none') should be checked against the Prakrit (khāmemi savva jīve, savve jīvā khamantu me, mittī me savva bhūesu, veraṃ majjha na keṇai).

Names of the day differ: Svetambara Jains commonly speak of Samvatsari at the end of Paryushana, Digambara Jains of Kshamavani after Das Lakshana. The voice says only that 'Jains call the closing day by more than one name'; a Keeper should confirm the wording and whether to mention both.
The meaning of micchami dukkadam is attributed to Jain explanation ('may my wrong be fruitless / in vain'); confirm the gloss and the Devanagari spelling.
'Prakrit, the old language of the Jain scriptures' (Ardhamagadhi Prakrit for the Svetambara canon): confirm.
